newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia and Chechnya trade harsh words over blasts.
newsitem.headline: Russia and Chechnya trade harsh words over blasts.

text.p: Russian and Chechen separatist leaders traded angry accusations on Tuesday over bombings and other violent incidents, raising tensions to their bitterest pitch since a ceasefire reached last August.

But Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin made clear that the Kremlin wanted to preserve the truce, which ended nearly 21 months of war, despite two fatal bomb attacks and a reported clash between police and rebels.
Russian police fought a brief night skirmish with a group of what they said were 20 Chechen fighters just outside Chechnya, resulting in casualties on both sides.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said police had detained two Chechen women fighters suspected of organising a bombing which killed two people and wounded more than 20 at a railway station in the south Russian spa resort of Pyatigorsk on Monday.
He told a news conference the two were part of a Chechen armed group which attacked the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995 and took hostages. More than 100 people were killed in the attack.

Russian news agencies quoted police sources as saying the Pyatigorsk attack was similar to a bomb blast at a railway station in the southern Russian town of Armavir last Wednesday which killed two people.
Kulikov demanded tough measures to counteract terrorism.
"These are not rebels. This is not a political struggle," he said. "This is banditry. We will catch and destroy those criminals."

His accusations were immediately denied by Chechen Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov, Itar-Tass news agency said. The separatist leaders accused unnamed Russian special services of planting the bomb to disrupt peacemaking.
Chechen Vice-President Vakha Arsanov, quoted by Interfax news agency, said talks on political matters were impossible until Kulikov apologised for his allegations or proved them.
The latest tensions seemed to open differences in Moscow over how to handle Chechnya.

Chernomyrdin, speaking at a news conference in the Slovak capital Bratislava, condemned the Pyatigorsk attack but focused on the need to preserve negotiations with the rebels, in contrast with Kulikov's harsh words.

"Terror is vandalism and innocent people die," he said. "But our relations toward the (peace) treaty will not be affected by this...the Chechen leadership has denied any connection with these terrorist attacks."
The ceasefire signed last August halted fighting but did not resolve the main dispute -- whether the rebel region is part of Russia or independent.
They two sides are now involved in difficult negotiations over a long-term peace treaty intended to open the way for Moscow's help in rebuilding war-shattered Chechnya.
Boris Berezovsky, a senior aide to President Boris Yeltsin who is heavily involved in shuttle diplomacy with Chechnya, appealed for restraint.
"Irresponsible statements are being made today by those who have not had enough of the war in Chechnya," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
Russian news agencies reported that Udugov and Berezovsky, a deputy head of Yeltsin's policy-making Security Council, agreed that peace talks should go ahead.
Tass said Yeltsin, on vacation at the Black Sea resort of Sochi, was expected to meet Kulikov on Wednesday for a detailed review of the situation in southern Russia.
Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Tass the president was extremely concerned and wanted law and order bodies to take the "most tough and resolute...actions".
